The CI-monitor session confirmed that the October 9 fuzz-ticket session is closed, so #2184, #2928 and #3093 have no active agent. Their assignments stay as they are. Its implementer has my five C# findings and the gap-digest finding, and is reworking #6296 to address them. It will send a corrected patch for a focused re-review when it's ready.

No reply is needed. Nothing is waiting on me until that patch arrives.

The earlier reviewer is closed, so I'll start a fresh one, pointed at its prior report so it knows the six findings. First I'll rebuild the corrected tree from the new full patch on its stated base, `e638bb9`:
The corrected patch applies cleanly to `e638bb9`, changing 21 files. The earlier reviewer's report directory is empty after closing, so I'll put the six prior findings into the new brief myself:
My message to the CI-monitor session left a placeholder where the reviewer's id should be. Sending the correction:

I've added the CI-monitor session's suspected same-name twin defect to the second reviewer's checks. The concern: `App/Twin.cs` and `Loose/Twin.cs` share the FQN `Twin` but have different members. A call to `OnlyOutside()` might then be answered completely from the Loose copy, even though Loose is in no compilation. The current test may not catch this, because it gives both twins the same member. The reviewer will also trace the case where configuration proves Loose is excluded, and will call the defect confirmed only if its own trace is decisive.

Waiting on its verdict.

The second review blocks the corrected patch. Four of the six prior findings are fixed (2, 4, 5 and 6), and so is the explicit-include part of finding 3. Three blocking defects remain, all ending in a complete answer that could be wrong:
- **B1, same-name twin (the CI-monitor session's suspicion, confirmed by trace).** The unresolved twin is removed from the unproven set (`graph_support.rs:1610-1618`), while member lookup searches by FQN without filtering (`get_definition/csharp.rs:4325-4335`). So `s.Work()` resolves to a member that exists only in the Loose copy. The corrected twin test expects that `Resolved`, so it encodes the defect.
- **B2, inheritance.** The new guard checks only the returned definition's parent chain (`:1148-1158`). `x.Hum()` on an unproven `Lonely : Base` resolves to `Base.Hum`.
- **B3, ignored SDK-glob sources.** The default glob compiles an ignored `Generated/Globals.cs`, but the no-globals proof only checks explicit includes. A previously incomplete answer becomes Complete.

One item is a scope decision rather than a defect. Qualified, `global::` and alias paths were already unfiltered before this patch, but they can still produce positive answers, which breaks the "stays incomplete or Unresolved" rule. Whoever owns #6296 decides whether the contract excludes them. Sending the verdict:

The second #6296 review is delivered to the CI-monitor session, and the verdict is still blocking. Four of the six original findings are fixed, and finding 3 is fixed for explicit includes. Three defects remain, each able to produce a confident wrong answer:
- **B1, same-name twin:** a member that exists only in an out-of-compilation copy resolves completely, and the corrected test expects that result. This confirms the CI-monitor session's suspicion.
- **B2, inheritance:** a member inherited through an unproven class (`Lonely : Base`) still resolves completely.
- **B3, ignored SDK-glob sources:** the default glob compiles an ignored `Globals.cs` that the global-usings proof never sees, so a previously incomplete answer becomes Complete.

One scope decision is flagged for #6296's owner (David, or you). Qualified, `global::` and alias paths can still return positive answers. That breaks the "stays incomplete or Unresolved" rule, so the contract either has to exclude those paths explicitly, with an open issue, or extend the same uncertainty to them.

I closed the reviewer and removed the scratch worktree. The full findings are in my message to the CI-monitor session, which owns the fixes.

Both reviewers left empty report directories; their sandboxes likely couldn't write there. Their full record was the handback each returned to me. I've saved both verbatim beside the CI-monitor session's review inputs, recording the exact tree each one reviewed, and sent it the paths:
- `second-review-3ab6aee5-handback.md` in `ci-watch-review-20261022-0300/`
- `first-review-c5a0e383-handback.md` in `ci-watch-review-20261022-0100/`

The CI-monitor session accepted the blocking verdict and settled the open scope question with your standing repair mandate and David's existing comment. Qualified, `global::` and alias paths get the same honest uncertainty, with no narrowing of the contract. For B3, it uses a durable record of every input, or otherwise keeps the old incomplete answers and drops the two unsupported Complete assertions. That matches what the review asked for.

The implementer is fixing B1–B3. I'll re-review when the CI-monitor session sends the fixed patch; nothing else is waiting on me.

Third read-only review of #6296. I'll follow the same flow: rebuild the tree from the new patch on its stated base, `af0aa979`, then run a fresh reviewer that knows B1–B3 and the earlier findings. Earlier reviewers couldn't write their report directories, so I'll ask for the full findings in the handback and save it myself.

The third review blocks again, but its three findings are narrower. The exact B1, B2 and B3 counterexamples are fixed. The new findings are routes around those fixes:
1. **Static, qualified and `global::` receivers:** they go through the old unfiltered type helper, so `global::Lonely.Hum()` resolves completely through an unproven `Lonely`. The new `global::` test uses a parameter, so it misses this path.
2. **Twins and inheritance:** a proven `Twin` in App can still inherit `Base.Hum` through the unproven Loose twin's `: Base`, because base lists are read from every physical part.
3. **Overloads in the inverted graph:** eligibility checks only the FQN (`inverted.rs:212`, `|_| true`), so App's zero-argument `Work()` "proves" the outside `Work(int)`.

The six controls do test their claimed paths, but none covers these three. Saving the handback, then reporting:

The third #6296 review is delivered to the CI-monitor session, and it is still blocking. The previous round's exact counterexamples (B1, B2, B3) are fixed, but three routes around those fixes still produce a confident wrong answer:
1. **Static, qualified and `global::` receivers:** they go through the old unfiltered type helper, so `global::Lonely.Hum()` resolves completely through an unproven `Lonely`.
2. **Twins and inheritance:** a proven `Twin` can still inherit `Base.Hum` through the unproven twin's base list.
3. **Overloads in the inverted graph:** a visible `Work()` "proves" an outside `Work(int)`, because eligibility checks only the FQN.

All three have the same cause. Some lookup still decides eligibility by FQN, or through a helper that never checks the physical declaration's membership. I suggested routing every receiver, base-list and member path through one membership-aware candidate source rather than patching each call site.

I also checked the CI-monitor session's late variant myself; the reviewer had already closed. `identity_visibility` (`graph_support.rs:394`) does count any matching declaration with the same name and signature. I classed that case as existing identity conflation that master also has, not a failure of this PR. Bifrost's member identity has no project component, so the PR shouldn't claim attribution to a specific physical copy for identical-signature twins. It should list that as a limitation.

The handback is saved verbatim at `ci-watch-review-20261022-0500/third-review-b2611f0f-handback.md`. The reviewer is closed and the scratch worktree removed; nothing is waiting on me.

The CI-monitor session accepted the third review and agrees with the centralized fix: one membership-aware source for receiver, base-list and member candidates, instead of patches at each call site. It sent all three counterexamples and the same-signature variant to the original implementer.

The implementer must show that its new tests fail on the old head and pass on the new one, and must keep legitimate partial-type and external evidence. Then it returns a clean full patch for a fresh review. No reply is needed. I'll review that patch when it arrives; nothing else is waiting on me.

The CI-monitor session chose option A, strict uncertainty, and accepted that "Directory.Build.props/<Import> make ordinary answers incomplete." That could cut C# coverage widely, because most modern .NET repos have a `Directory.Build.props`. It could also break the C# calibration expectations that #5682 depends on. I'll check whether the pinned benchmark C# corpora contain such files, and whether their selectors expect `resolved`:

I sent the CI monitor a warning about option A. It is a request to measure before accepting, not a new review.

**The risk.** Under option A, a C# answer becomes incomplete whenever a `Directory.Build.props` or an `<Import>` makes project membership unprovable. The pinned Dapper calibration checkout has these files:
- `Directory.Build.props` and `Directory.Build.targets` at the root
- more of them in `tests/` and `benchmarks/`
- `Directory.Packages.props`

`benchmark/targets.toml` expects `Dapper/SqlMapper.cs:1862:28` (`CacheInfo`) to resolve to `Dapper.SqlMapper$CacheInfo`. The location and usage scenarios for the same symbol depend on that answer too.

If option A turns those Directory.Build gaps into Unresolved membership for Dapper's files, that calibration expectation will fail. Whether it actually fails is unknown until someone runs it. It depends on whether looking up a nested type inside the partial `SqlMapper` checks compilation visibility. More broadly, most modern multi-project .NET repositories have a `Directory.Build.props`, so option A could move many ordinary C# answers from resolved to incomplete, compared with master.

**What I asked for.** Before the patch lands, the worker should measure two things:
1. The Dapper calibration target, on master and on the candidate.
2. A before-and-after count of how many type and member reference answers change status in Dapper.

If the loss is broad, it is a product tradeoff for you or David to decide explicitly. It should not ship as a routine consequence of the "no complete answer without evidence" rule.

**A narrower alternative.** Read the Directory.Build settings that change membership, such as `EnableDefaultCompileItems` and `Compile` include and remove items. Treat them as evaluated inputs. Record a gap only for constructs we cannot evaluate.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The three #6296 reviews kept finding the same kind of bug. A file whose project membership was unproven still yielded a Resolved answer, through a path the membership filter did not cover: a twin type with the same name, an inherited member, or a `global::` receiver. Option A fixes this by making every unproven case incomplete. That is sound, but it costs coverage wherever membership is hard to prove.
- Directory.Build files are where this cost lands. MSBuild applies them to every project below them in the directory tree, so one root file affects the whole repository. If the analyzer cannot evaluate that one file, every C# file in the repository loses its membership proof.
- Calibration targets such as the Dapper `CacheInfo` entry are a cheap way to check this. A single expected-resolved answer in a real repository shows whether a soundness change is too strict, before anyone needs a corpus-wide census.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Nothing else is open on my side. I'm waiting for the CI monitor's next clean #6296 patch and its control test results so I can re-review it.

The CI monitor agreed to measure the impact before #6342 lands. The pull request stays a draft until two things are done: a fresh review, and a measured impact assessment. The assessment covers the Dapper `CacheInfo` calibration target on master and on the candidate, plus a small count of how many type and member answers change status. If the existing proof code cannot keep the intended coverage without claiming completeness it cannot prove, the monitor will bring the measured tradeoff to you then.

I sent them the corpus details:
- **Checkout to use:** `/mnt/optane/tmp/calib-5682/dapper`. It is at the pinned commit `72a54c475f` from `benchmark/targets.toml:459-461`, its working tree is clean, and it has 157 `.cs` files.
- **Checkout to avoid:** `dapper-bom-stripped`. It is an earlier diagnostic copy with one modified test file and a leftover `.bifrost` cache.
- **No second C# corpus:** Dapper is the only C# repository in `targets.toml`, and I found no other C# project checkout in local scratch. A second corpus would need a fresh clone.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- With only one C# repository in the calibration corpus, the "too strict" risk has thin coverage. One repository's Directory.Build layout says little about how common unevaluable MSBuild constructs are elsewhere. The count from Dapper will show whether the problem exists; it will not show how often it occurs across real repositories.
- Earlier passes left a stale diagnostic copy and old `xdg-dapper-diagnose-*` caches in the same folder as the clean checkout. If the before-and-after measurement reused one of those caches, it would compare against results from an older binary, so I asked for a fresh `XDG_CACHE_HOME` on each side.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Nothing is waiting on you. I'm waiting for the CI monitor's next clean #6296 patch and the impact numbers.
